title: Financial Policy Committee Record – April 2026
summary: The FPC met on 27 March 2026 and judged that the Middle East conflict has caused a substantial negative supply shock to the global economy, triggering significant volatility in energy prices and government bond yields. Multiple financial stability vulnerabilities could crystallize simultaneously, including in sovereign debt markets, risky asset valuations, and private credit. The Committee maintained the UK CCyB at 2%, assessed the banking system as appropriately capitalized and resilient, and found no evidence of lending restrictions.
key_points: The Middle East conflict has caused a substantial negative supply shock, increasing inflation, weighing on growth, and tightening financial conditions globally
FPC maintained the UK countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) rate at 2%, noting the banking system remains appropriately capitalized with high liquidity and strong asset quality

Sovereign debt markets face elevated risks: historically high issuance with higher proportions at shorter maturities, and leveraged hedge fund positions pursuing similar strategies across jurisdictions
Repo markets have functioned well and absorbed high volatility and volumes so far, providing market structure resilience
Private credit markets show elevated redemption requests in international retail funds, with some funds limiting redemptions, highlighting liquidity mismatch and valuation concerns
US technology companies focused on AI face stretched valuations given debt-financing needs, uncertain AI investment returns, and energy-intensive supply chains
FPC supports the Private Markets System-Wide Exploratory Scenario (PM SWES) to explore risks from banks and NBFIs in private markets
Financial system has not yet adopted advanced AI (generative or agentic) in a manner presenting systemic risk, but risks may increase as firms expand AI deployment
why_it_matters: This FPC record provides the official assessment of systemic risks facing the UK financial system following a major geopolitical shock. Market participants should note the Committee's emphasis on multiple vulnerabilities potentially crystallizing simultaneously, particularly in private credit and sovereign debt markets, and incorporate stress testing scenarios for sudden market dislocations. The functioning of repo markets is identified as critical to market resilience.
macro_context: The conflict has created a negative supply shock that will weigh on global growth, increase inflation, and tighten financial conditions. This increases the likelihood that sovereign debt vulnerabilities, compressed risk premia, and private credit concerns could amplify each other if conditions worsen.
market_structure_context: Repo markets have functioned as a stabilizing force absorbing high volatility and volumes. However, sovereign debt markets are characterized by high leverage among a small number of hedge funds pursuing similar strategies, creating risk of disorderly unwind and jump-to-illiquidity dynamics. Global equity and debt risk premia remain compressed by historical standards despite elevated volatility.
